extracted.intended_audience: aspiring writers, literary students, educated readers and critics interested in the role and responsibilities of the Man of Letters
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts guidance and evaluative criteria about what constitutes a genuine 'Man of Letters' (the literary hero): his vocation, qualities, social role, and the conditions that produce or impede him. The lecture treats both moral/aesthetic standards for writers and social/organizational commentary about literary life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proclaiming the Divine Idea
rubrics_metrics.description: The Man of Letters is sent specially to discern for himself, and make manifest to us, the 'Divine Idea of the World' which lies at the bottom of Appearance; he unfolds the Godlike in the terrestrial and common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from Fichte's formulation quoted in the lecture: the literary man’s vocation is prophetic/priestly — to reveal the inward, eternal reality beneath superficial appearances. Examples/figures evoked include Goethe as someone who embodied this function. The writer's work should thereby aim at unveiling the 'open secret' rather than merely treating surface trivialities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspiration / Originality / Sincerity (the 'heroic' quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: What we call 'originality,' 'sincerity,' 'genius' — the heroic quality — is essentially being 'inspired'; the Hero is he who lives in the inward sphere of things and declares that abroad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle equates the heroic literary quality with an inner inspiration: writers must be inwardly authoritative and sincere. This is the intrinsic test of greatness (he cites 'originality, sincerity, genius' as names for that quality). Practical implication: evaluate writers by whether their work springs from an authentic inner vision rather than imitation or mere craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity: live wholly in the Divine Idea
rubrics_metrics.description: A true Literary Man must live wholly in the Divine Idea; whoever lives not wholly (or only partially) in this is a 'Bungler', 'Stumper', or 'Nonentity' according to Fichte — not a Literary Man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lecture stresses a binary authenticity test: partial or performative engagement with profundity is insufficient. The guidance is severe: genuine literary heroism requires sustained, whole-hearted devotion to the inward truth; mere technical skill or social success does not qualify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence and Responsibility (writers shape the world)
rubrics_metrics.description: What a Man of Letters teaches, the whole world will do and make; the writer’s teaching has vast social force — the writer is effectively a branch of government, a 'Fourth Estate'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because printed words govern taste, law, morals and practice, writers carry civic and moral responsibility. Carlyle repeatedly argues that literature functions as pulpit, senate, and parliament: assess writers by the extent and nature of their influence and by whether they responsibly guide public life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness and Order (literature as revelation of truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Order is Truth; literature should be an 'apocalypse of Nature' revealing the 'open secret' — Books should report truly and not propagate smooth Falsehoods or superficialities that become disorder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle warns that books exert practical consequences (he gives examples of novels shaping conduct). A key evaluative criterion is whether a book reveals deep truth and promotes intellectual/ moral order rather than spreading falsity or trivial illusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature as Worship (moving the heart toward the Godlike)
rubrics_metrics.description: All true singing (literature) is of the nature of worship: a gifted literary work brings melody into hearts and makes visible the 'handwriting' of the Maker; it is akin to touching the heart 'with a live coal from the altar.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate literary works by their ability to evoke sacredness, beauty and moral elevation in readers. Carlyle names Milton, Shakespeare (Shakspeare), Goethe, Burns as varying exemplars — from cathedral music to humble skylark-notes — all valid when they consecrate the reader's inner life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for Struggle and Poverty as Schooling
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience of outward poverty, contradiction, sorrow and degradation can be necessary schooling for a genuine literary man; poverty can be formative rather than merely pitiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle suggests poverty and struggle test and train a writer's authenticity (Johnson and Burns are cited). This is a normative criterion for the production of genuine literature: evaluate whether the writer’s hardships have contributed to moral depth and honesty rather than mere affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Durability: spirit over letter
rubrics_metrics.description: The letter of a man's work may die but the spirit of it never; a genuine literary achievement is judged by its enduring spiritual influence rather than by immediate reward or contemporary success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess works for enduring moral/spiritual force (the 'spirit') that outlives contemporaneous fashion or immediate material success. Carlyle praises those whose 'works have not died' despite hardships in life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization, Recognition and Social Provision for Men of Letters
rubrics_metrics.description: The present chaotic, disorganized condition of literary life is detrimental; Men of Letters ought to be recognized, organized and suitably facilitated — mere grants of money are not the whole solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle prescribes societal/institutional criteria: judging literary culture involves assessing whether society treats writers as an important public class, provides meaningful structural support (beyond cash), and arranges fair ordeals for recognition. He cites nascent arrangements in France, Prussia and the Chinese attempt to integrate literary talent into governance as relevant examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Books as the True Vehicle of Teaching (writers must account for their educative role)
rubrics_metrics.description: With the art of Writing and Printing, Books have become the primary medium of teaching; the 'true University' of modern times is a collection of books — hence a writer's role is essentially pedagogic and public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate writers by their awareness of books' educational reach and by how effectively their printed work communicates and instructs distant readers. Carlyle also contrasts the remaining province of speech (lectures) with the unique ubiquity and permanence of books, implying writers should craft with that reach and permanence in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to Persuade and Practical Consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Books and printed words persuade and have concrete practical consequences in daily life (even 'wretched circulating-library novels' influence household behaviours); therefore the moral effect of what a writer publishes is a key evaluative dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess literary works by their real-world effects — positive or negative — on conduct, institutions, and beliefs. Carlyle uses examples ('Celia', 'Clifford') to show how fiction can translate into practice; writers must be judged for the practical persuasiveness of their texts.
